question: What does the acronym CI stand for in the context of software development?

options.text: Container Infrastructure — container-based infrastructure
options.explanation: Container Infrastructure is not a standard DevOps term, and CI does not directly relate to containers

options.text: Code Inspection — automated code quality checking
options.explanation: Code Inspection refers to static code analysis, which may be part of CI but is not its definition

options.text: Continuous Improvement — ongoing process improvement
options.explanation: Continuous Improvement is a quality management concept (Kaizen), not from DevOps

options.text: Continuous Integration — continuous code integration
options.explanation: CI is the practice of frequently integrating code from all developers with automated checks via tests and linters

question: What is the key difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

options.text: In Continuous Delivery, production deployment is manually approved; in Continuous Deployment, it is automatic
options.explanation: Continuous Delivery — the code is always ready to deploy, but a human makes the final decision. Continuous Deployment — every green commit is automatically deployed to production

options.text: Continuous Delivery works only with Docker, Continuous Deployment works with any infrastructure
options.explanation: Both approaches are independent of deployment technology and work with any infrastructure

options.text: In Continuous Delivery, production deployment happens automatically; in Continuous Deployment, it is manual
options.explanation: It is the opposite: Continuous Deployment automates production deployment, while Delivery requires a manual button press

options.text: Continuous Delivery is for small teams, Continuous Deployment is for large teams
options.explanation: The choice between them depends on testing maturity and business requirements, not team size

question: What is a feedback loop in the context of CI/CD?

options.text: The time between writing code and receiving information about whether it works correctly
options.explanation: The shorter the feedback loop, the faster a developer learns about a bug, and the cheaper it is to fix — context is still fresh

options.text: A mechanism for re-running failed pipelines
options.explanation: Re-running is a retry mechanism, not a feedback loop

options.text: The retrospective cycle in Agile teams
options.explanation: Retrospectives are an Agile practice, and while they are a form of feedback, in CI/CD the term is used differently

options.text: A system for collecting user feedback about the product
options.explanation: Collecting user feedback is a UX practice, not a CI/CD concept

question: Which of the following problems are characteristic of manual deployment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Losing the backup before deployment
options.explanation: With manual deployment it is easy to skip the backup step, especially under time pressure

options.text: Difficulty reproducing the deployment process by another person
options.explanation: With manual deployment, knowledge of the process is often stored in one person's head or in outdated instructions

options.text: Slow feedback on the deployment result
options.explanation: After manual deployment there are often no automated checks — you have to manually verify everything works

options.text: Impossibility of automated testing
options.explanation: Tests can still be run with manual deployment; these are two independent processes

options.text: High risk of human error
options.explanation: Manual processes are prone to typos, forgotten steps, and incorrect sequence of actions

question: A team is adopting CI/CD for the first time. They plan to set it up after releasing the main features. What is wrong with this approach?

options.text: CI/CD is harder to set up on a large project, and technical debt and the number of potential issues grow
options.explanation: Setting up CI/CD from the first commit takes 30 minutes. On a project with a year of history it can take days: you need to sort out dependencies, tests, and environment configuration

options.text: GitHub Actions is only free for public repositories
options.explanation: While this is a true statement, it does not answer the question about the problem with the 'set it up later' approach

options.text: CI/CD is not suitable for early-stage projects
options.explanation: On the contrary, CI/CD is especially valuable at the early stage — it establishes good practices from the very beginning

options.text: Nothing, this is reasonable prioritization — business value first, infrastructure later
options.explanation: In practice, 'later' rarely comes. Moreover, setting up CI/CD on a large codebase with accumulated technical debt is significantly harder

question: What is an artifact in the context of a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: An environment variable available across all jobs
options.explanation: Environment variables are configuration, not artifacts

options.text: A pipeline execution log
options.explanation: Logs are stored separately and are not artifacts in the classical sense — they are not passed between stages as a result of work

options.text: Documentation automatically generated from code
options.explanation: Documentation can be an artifact, but it is only one of many types of artifacts

options.text: The result of one pipeline stage that is passed to the next stage
options.explanation: An artifact is any file or set of files created during the pipeline: a compiled binary, a Docker image, a test report

question: Which of the following CI/CD tools are SaaS solutions (do not require your own server)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Jenkins
options.explanation: Jenkins is a self-hosted solution that requires its own server for installation and maintenance

options.text: A special license is required for this
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

options.text: CircleCI
options.explanation: CircleCI is a cloud service provided by subscription, does not require your own infrastructure

options.text: GitLab CI (GitLab.com)
options.explanation: GitLab.com is a SaaS variant of GitLab with built-in CI/CD. A self-hosted GitLab also exists

options.text: GitHub Actions
options.explanation: GitHub Actions is a cloud service built into GitHub, does not require its own infrastructure (although self-hosted runners are possible)

question: In what order are pipeline stages typically executed?

options.text: Test → Source → Build → Deploy
options.explanation: Tests are run after the build, because many tests need a built artifact

options.text: Source → Deploy → Test → Build
options.explanation: Deploying before testing is a dangerous practice that should be avoided

options.text: Source → Build → Test → Deploy
options.explanation: First get the code (Source/Checkout), then build the artifact (Build), verify its correctness (Test), and only then deploy (Deploy)

options.text: Deploy → Test → Build → Source
options.explanation: This is the reverse order: you cannot deploy what has not been built and tested

question: Why is a slow pipeline (40+ minutes) harmful to a team?

options.text: A slow pipeline always means bad code
options.explanation: Pipeline speed depends on its configuration, not code quality. Good code can have a slow pipeline due to suboptimal configuration

options.text: The feedback loop slows down — bugs are found too late
options.explanation: If a developer switches to another task during 40 minutes, context is lost and fixing a bug takes significantly more time

options.text: This is only possible in cloud solutions
options.explanation: This applies both in the cloud and on-premise.

options.text: The cost of using cloud CI/CD services increases
options.explanation: Most cloud CI/CD services charge by job execution time. Slow pipelines = more expenses

options.text: Developers start ignoring the pipeline and looking for workarounds
options.explanation: When you have to wait 40 minutes for every commit, developers start merging without waiting for the result, which defeats the purpose of CI

question: What is the correct way to store secrets (API keys, passwords) in CI/CD configuration?

options.text: In commit comments, closed to external users
options.explanation: Secrets in commit comments are a critical security vulnerability. No access restriction makes this acceptable

options.text: In CI/CD system environment variables or in specialized vault services
options.explanation: GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI Variables, HashiCorp Vault — these are the correct places for secrets. They are encrypted and do not end up in the repository

options.text: Directly in the YAML pipeline configuration file, encrypted with base64
options.explanation: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the value. Secrets must not be stored in the repository

options.text: In a separate private repository
options.explanation: A private repository is not sufficient protection: secrets will be visible to everyone with repo access and will end up in git history

question: What is a trigger in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: The first pipeline stage that downloads code
options.explanation: Code checkout is a step inside the pipeline, not the event that starts it

options.text: A developer responsible for running the deployment
options.explanation: A trigger is an event, not a person

options.text: An event that starts the pipeline execution
options.explanation: Triggers can be: a push to the repository, creating a pull request, a schedule (cron), a manual run, or completion of another pipeline

options.text: A condition under which the pipeline stops with an error
options.explanation: A stop condition is a fail condition or exit code, not a trigger

question: A team is working on a banking application. Which deployment approach should they choose?

options.text: No CI/CD at all — security requirements are too high
options.explanation: CI/CD improves security through automated checks, vulnerability scanning, and a predictable process. A manual process is more vulnerable

options.text: Jenkins, because it is the oldest and most proven
options.explanation: The choice of tool does not determine the deployment approach. Jenkins can be configured for both Delivery and Deployment

options.text: Continuous Delivery — code is always ready for deployment, but the deployment decision is made manually
options.explanation: Banking systems require controlled releases: compliance, auditing, manual approval. Continuous Delivery provides CI automation + control over final deployment

options.text: Continuous Deployment — every commit is automatically deployed to production
options.explanation: For banking software, manual deployment approval is usually required for compliance and security reasons. Full automation without manual control is risky here

question: Which statements about jobs within a single pipeline stage are correct?

options.text: Jobs always run strictly sequentially
options.explanation: Jobs run in parallel unless explicit dependencies (needs/depends_on) are specified. This is one of the advantages of CI/CD systems

options.text: Each job runs in an isolated environment
options.explanation: Each job runs in its own container or virtual machine. This ensures reproducibility and isolation

options.text: Jobs within one stage can run in parallel
options.explanation: Parallel execution of jobs within one stage is standard practice to speed up the pipeline. For example, unit tests and e2e tests can be run simultaneously

options.text: A special license is required for this
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

options.text: The next stage starts only after all jobs in the current stage are complete
options.explanation: Stages run sequentially — this ensures that deployment does not start until all tests pass

question: A startup wants to quickly start using CI/CD. Which tool is the simplest option for a team already using GitHub?

options.text: Travis CI — the first open source tool
options.explanation: Travis CI no longer offers a free plan and has lost market share to GitHub Actions and GitLab CI

options.text: GitLab CI — the most powerful system
options.explanation: For a team on GitHub, switching to GitLab just for CI/CD is not practical. GitLab CI is a great tool, but not in this scenario

options.text: GitHub Actions — built into GitHub, minimal entry barrier
options.explanation: GitHub Actions does not require additional registration, is integrated with the repository, has a huge marketplace of ready-made actions, and has a clear syntax

options.text: Jenkins — the most proven and flexible tool
options.explanation: Jenkins requires its own server, complex setup, and maintenance. For a startup this is excessive complexity

question: What does 'a broken pipeline is priority #1' mean?

options.text: A broken pipeline automatically reverts the last commit
options.explanation: Rollback is an optional setting. Most CI/CD systems do not do automatic rollback by default

options.text: You cannot merge new code until the pipeline is fixed
options.explanation: A broken pipeline means no one is getting feedback. Continuing to merge means multiplying problems and losing the signal about code state

options.text: The entire team should know about the broken pipeline immediately
options.explanation: Notifications in Slack/email when the pipeline fails are standard practice. The problem must be visible to everyone so it is fixed quickly

options.text: Fixing a broken pipeline is more important than working on new features
options.explanation: Analogy: if the conveyor belt stops — you need to fix it first, not keep throwing parts into a pile
